name: Treaty with the S'Klallam, 1855 (Treaty of Point No Point)
nations: S'Klallam (nəxʷsƛ̕ay̕əm̕): Port Gamble, Jamestown and Lower Elwha
promises: Article 2 reserved six sections, 3,840 acres, at the head of Hood Canal for the tribes' exclusive use, closed to white residents without permission.
Article 4 secured the right of taking fish at usual and accustomed grounds and stations in common with all citizens, with hunting and gathering on open and unclaimed lands.
Article 11: an agricultural and industrial school, a smithy and carpenter's shop, and a physician for twenty years.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the 438,430 acres the S'Klallam ceded had a fair market value of $440,000 and that the consideration allocable to them under the treaty, $43,098, was unconscionable.

breaches.what: In the case the United States brought in 1970, which names the Treaty of Point No Point, the Port Gamble and Lower Elwha Clallam and the Skokomish, the Supreme Court upheld the ruling that the treaty fishing clause secures the tribes a share of the fish, and recorded that the State Game Department refused to comply with the federal decree.

breaches.what: The Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe says the S'Klallam were assigned to the Skokomish reservation over 100 miles from their homes, many refused to go, and 67 years after the treaty they still had no land base.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe, History page

landTaken: 438,430 acres ceded by the S'Klallam (ICC Docket 134) and 355,800 acres ceded by the Skokomish (ICC Docket 296, 1961 conclusion as restated in 1963). The Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe describes the whole cession as about three quarters of a million acres.
compensation: S'Klallam: $385,820 final award (1976). Skokomish: $373,577 by compromise settlement (1963), which was not a finding of unconscionability.
today: The treaty fishing right is enforced under the continuing jurisdiction of United States v. Washington.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the talks were held in Chinook Jargon, that the S'Klallam were sent toward the distant Skokomish reservation, and that decades later they still had no land of their own.

plain.promised: 3,840 acres at the head of Hood Canal for the tribes' exclusive use, the right of taking fish at usual and accustomed grounds, $60,000 over twenty years, and a school, physician and shops.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1970 that the $43,098 allocated for the S'Klallam's 438,430 acres, worth $440,000, was unconscionable. The Supreme Court recorded in 1979 that Washington's Game Department refused to comply with the treaty fishing decree.
plain.today: The S'Klallam were awarded $385,820 in 1976, and the Skokomish settled for $373,577 in 1963. Whether these were paid has not been traced. The fishing right is enforced under United States v. Washington.

openQuestions: The 1970 S'Klallam decision itself (23 Ind. Cl. Comm. 510) was not opened; its findings are taken from the Commission's 1976 restatement. The 1976 motion turned on whether $15,000 or $39,180 was paid.
The Port Gamble S'Klallam history mentions a 1925 settlement of $400,000; its legal basis was not identified and it is not recorded as compensation here.
The list of tribes in the culvert proceeding was not confirmed from the Ninth Circuit opinion, which could not be opened.

Audit 2026-11-08: removed the 2018 culvert breach. Neither the CRS sidebar nor the Ninth Circuit opinion (853 F.3d 946, read through the copy the researcher cited) names the Treaty of Point No Point or its tribes; they speak of 'the Stevens Treaties' and 'the Tribes', and the only treaty named is Medicine Creek. It was carried over from a sibling file. If the Port Gamble, Lower Elwha, Jamestown or Skokomish tribes are shown to be plaintiffs in the culvert subproceeding, it can come back. The CRS report stays as context. The 1979 Fishing Vessel ruling does name this treaty (12 Stat. 933) and the Port Gamble, Lower Elwha and Skokomish tribes, so it stays. ICC figures held.
